title: Low Sugars Without Diabetes in a Bus Driver / Catch the Episode, Stop the Driving

blocks.text: Low Sugars Without Diabetes in a Bus Driver / Catch the Episode, Stop the Driving

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-13 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: Endocrine Society: Evaluation and management of adult hypoglycemic disorders (2009), as summarised in Endotext (updated 5 October 2025); DVLA: Diabetes mellitus, assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025); JBDS 01 Hospital management of hypoglycaemia in adults with diabetes mellitus (2023 revision); GMC: Confidentiality: patients' fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017) · Related AMaC: None identified

Dear Doctor, a 44-year-old bus driver. Six months of episodes of sweating, shaking and confusion, usually before breakfast. A paramedic recorded a glucose of 2.3 mmol/litre last month, and it rose after a sugary drink. He does not have diabetes. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Episodes of low glucose that settle with sugar, in a man without diabetes, are hypoglycaemia until a cause is found. The station turns on proving it with a sample taken during an episode, and on stopping a bus driver driving.

The Examiner Trap. He still drives his bus and treats the episodes with sweets. Candidates organise tests and say nothing about driving, or send him home to fast. Pass: Whipple's triad, a supervised critical sample, no driving, DVLA. Fail: driving allowed.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Ask about the episodes, then about food, drugs, alcohol, family history and his job.
"What happens during an episode, and when? Does sugar fix it? Do you take any tablets, injections or alcohol? What do you drive?"
Timing; symptoms; relief; weight; drugs; insulin in the household; alcohol; surgery; family history; driving.
Look for causes and for signs of other endocrine disease, and check the abdomen.
"May I check your blood pressure, your hands and face, your neck and your abdomen? Tell me if anything hurts."
Weight; acromegaly; adrenal signs; liver stigmata; abdomen scars; lymph nodes; fundi; cover him.
Explain that the sample during an episode is the key test, say what you suspect, and give clear driving advice.
"Your sugar drops too low and I need to catch it in hospital. Please don't drive your bus. You must tell the DVLA yourself, and I'll help you."
Supervised fast; hormone tests; imaging; treatment; driving; glucose; return signs.

Asks timing, symptoms, relief with sugar, drugs, insulin or tablets at home, alcohol and driving.
Also asks about family history of tumours, kidney stones and calcium problems, and whether others have seen an episode.

Focused examination
Omits the abdomen or the neck; reports tumour signs that are absent.
Finds weight gain, a normal abdomen with no scar, no hepatomegaly, no acromegalic features and no lymph nodes.
Also finds normal blood pressure, no adrenal signs and normal fundi.
R4
D
Differential diagnosis
Calls it panic attacks or reactive hypoglycaemia alone.
Hypoglycaemia from endogenous hyperinsulinism, most likely insulinoma.
Also names factitious insulin or sulfonylurea use, adrenal insufficiency, liver failure and alcohol, and says MEN1 is possible.

Tests
Repeats a fasting glucose in clinic.
Asks for a supervised 72-hour fast with a sample during an episode: glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a sulfonylurea screen.
Also asks for calcium, PTH and prolactin, then CT, MRI or endoscopic ultrasound after biochemistry.

E
Management and safety-net
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): lets him keep driving his bus, or arranges a fast at home alone.

Says stop driving now and that he must notify DVLA (the doctor informs DVLA only if he will not), take 15 to 20 g of fast sugar for an episode and recheck after 10 to 15 minutes, and call 999 if unrousable.
Also says to carry sugar and not to be alone, and that surgery can cure an insulinoma.

His concerns
Brushes aside his fear of losing his job and of a tumour.
Asks what worries him, acknowledges both and explains the tests will find the cause.
Also discusses his income, his employer and his fear of a collapse at work.

Shared plan
Tells him what to do with no choices.
Explains admission for a supervised fast within days, or a test during the next episode with urgent attendance, and asks his choice.
Records his choice, gives a written plan and a dated review.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 44-year-old bus driver. You are friendly, a little sheepish and worried about your job.
Opening line: "I keep getting these funny turns, sweaty and shaky and fuzzy in the head. A biscuit sorts it out. I've put on weight because I'm always eating."
Volunteered: six months. The turns come before breakfast or when you skip lunch.

Only if asked: once you were so confused a colleague thought you were drunk and had to give you a sugary drink. Non-smoker. You do not drink much. You take no tablets. No diabetes in the family that you know of.
Only if asked about driving: you drive a bus most days. You have never had an incident, but you felt woozy at the wheel last week and ate chocolate at the lights.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of crashing with passengers on board, and of losing your job. Say: "If I can't drive, I'm finished."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is it diabetes?" "Can I carry on driving?" "Is it a tumour?"
How you react: if told to stop driving with no support, you refuse. If listened to and offered a letter for work, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 132/82; temperature 36.6 °C. Weight up over the past year. Abdomen soft, no scars, no mass. No hepatomegaly. No acromegalic features. No lymphadenopathy. Fundi normal.

Results, only when requested: critical sample during a supervised fast and a symptomatic episode: plasma glucose below 3.0 mmol/litre; insulin raised; C-peptide raised; proinsulin raised; beta-hydroxybutyrate low; sulfonylurea screen negative. Calcium and prolactin normal. MRI: a small pancreatic lesion.
Question ladder: 1. What is Whipple's triad? (D) 2. What do you suspect? (D) 3. What do the results show? (D) 4. How do you treat the episode? (E) 5. What are the driving rules? (E)

Curveballs: He asks to fast at home: no; a supervised fast is safer. He asks if he can drive his car: stop driving and notify DVLA for severe hypoglycaemia (needing another person's help, as here) not caused by diabetes treatment, whichever licence he holds. He says he will not tell DVLA: the duty is his; make every reasonable effort to persuade him; if he keeps driving when unfit and this exposes others to a risk of death or serious harm, you will disclose relevant information promptly to the DVLA medical adviser, telling him beforehand where practicable and confirming in writing; document it (GMC, 2017). He becomes confused in clinic: urgent glucose, then the sample.
Introduces self, asks consent and asks about discomfort before examining (G)
Asks about timing, relief with sugar, drugs, insulin access and driving (C)
Examines the abdomen, neck and for acromegaly (A)
Finds weight gain and no signs of tumour or liver disease (B)
Names hypoglycaemia from endogenous hyperinsulinism, probably insulinoma (D)
Requests a supervised fast with a sample during an episode (E)
Names glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a sulfonylurea screen (E)
Says stop driving now and that he must tell DVLA (E)
Gives episode treatment and return signs (E)
Asks what worries him and offers, with his permission, a letter for work (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Lift your shirt. [R1 Fail] Panic attacks? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the abdomen.) [R3 Fail] It's anxiety. [R4 Fail] A fasting glucose in clinic. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Carry on driving, and fast at home. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] Come back in a year. [R8 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): the examiner sees a red flag, because a bus driver with unexplained hypoglycaemia must not drive, and a fast needs supervision. No consent, no examination, and anxiety assumed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I check your blood pressure, your abdomen and your neck? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: When do the turns come, and does sugar fix them? Any tablets, insulin at home or alcohol? What do you drive? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Before breakfast. A biscuit fixes it. I drive a bus.
CANDIDATE: (Examines, then covers him and thanks him.) Weight gain, a normal abdomen with no scar, no acromegalic features and no nodes. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I suspect hypoglycaemia from too much insulin, probably an insulinoma. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: A supervised hospital fast, sampling during an episode: glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a sulfonylurea screen. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: Don't drive, and you must tell DVLA yourself today; I'll help you. For an episode, take 15 to 20 g of fast sugar, check how you feel or your glucose after 10 to 15 minutes and repeat if still low; call 999 if you can't swallow or are drowsy. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: A crash, and my job.
CANDIDATE: Both are fair; with your permission I'll write a letter for your employer. [R7 Pass] We can admit you this week, or test at the next episode. Which do you prefer? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Gave driving and episode advice and planned a supervised test. Did not name other causes, calcium or MEN1 tests, or imaging.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll ask about alcohol and sex only with your permission. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any family history of tumours or kidney stones? Has anyone seen an episode? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Normal blood pressure, no adrenal signs, no lymph nodes. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Insulinoma; factitious insulin or sulfonylurea use, adrenal failure, liver failure and alcohol are other causes, and MEN1 is possible. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: Calcium, PTH and prolactin too, then CT, MRI or endoscopic ultrasound once the biochemistry is positive. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: Carry sugar and don't be alone; surgery can cure an insulinoma. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: With your permission I'll write to your employer, and we'll discuss your income. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and a review date. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, family history, other causes, MEN1 tests, imaging, surgery, a letter for work and a written plan.
R2: Not asking what he drives. A bus driver's licence is the main risk, and it decides the urgency.
R4: Calling it anxiety. Sweating, shaking and confusion that sugar fixes are hypoglycaemia until another cause is shown.
R5: Repeating a clinic glucose. A random fasting glucose misses the episode, so the diagnostic sample is never taken.
R6: Letting him keep driving. A bus driver with unexplained hypoglycaemia is a danger to passengers.
"Can I ask what you do for work, and whether you drive?"
"The turns settle with sugar, so I'd suspect hypoglycaemia."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

Endotext (updated 5 October 2025), adapted from Endocrine Society 2009: Whipple's triad is symptoms, a low plasma glucose (below 3.0 mmol/litre) and relief when glucose rises. Endogenous hyperinsulinism: insulin 18 pmol/litre (3 microunits/mL) or more, C-peptide 0.2 nmol/litre or more, proinsulin 5 pmol/litre or more, beta-hydroxybutyrate below 2.7 mmol/litre, and no sulfonylurea in the sample.

Treat a conscious episode with 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate by mouth, recheck glucose after 10 to 15 minutes and repeat up to three times (JBDS 01, 2023 revision, written for people with diabetes and used here as UK practice); if he cannot swallow safely, IV dextrose in hospital or 999. Surgical resection can be curative for insulinomas; medical options are diazoxide or octreotide.

DVLA (updated 7 November 2025): severe hypoglycaemia (needing another person's help) from causes other than diabetes treatment means stop driving and notify DVLA, car or bus. The driver must notify DVLA and stop driving; the doctor makes every reasonable effort to persuade him and, if he keeps driving when unfit and this exposes others to a risk of death or serious harm, discloses relevant information promptly to the DVLA medical adviser, telling him beforehand where practicable and confirming in writing, and documents it (GMC 2017). Bus licence: no severe episode in the previous 12 months is needed.
THINK: Low glucose without diabetes: think insulinoma.
SAY: "I need to catch your sugar during an episode."
DO: Ask what he drives; examine the abdomen.
NUMBERS: Glucose below 3.0 mmol/litre; C-peptide 0.2 nmol/litre or more.
TRAP: Driving; fasting at home.
FINISH: Supervised fast, DVLA, glucose for episodes, imaging.

Hypoglycemia. Endotext (updated 5 October 2025), Table 4 adapted from the Endocrine Society guideline, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2009. https://www.endotext.org/wp-content/uploads/pdfs/hypoglycemia.pdf Supports: Whipple's triad, diagnostic thresholds, supervised fast and insulinoma.

DVLA. Diabetes mellitus: assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025). https://www.gov.uk/guidance/diabetes-mellitus-assessing-fitness-to-drive Supports: Severe hypoglycaemia from non-diabetes causes: stop driving and notify DVLA; Group 2 relicensing conditions.

Joint British Diabetes Societies. JBDS 01: The hospital management of hypoglycaemia in adults with diabetes mellitus (revised January 2023; copy hosted by Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals), https://www.nnuh.nhs.uk/publication/download/hypoglycaemia-in-adults-with-diabetes-mellitus. Supports: 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate for a conscious person able to swallow, recheck after 10 to 15 minutes, repeat up to three times.

General Medical Council. Confidentiality: patients' fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017). https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/the-professional-standards/confidentiality---patients-fitness-to-drive-and-reporting-concerns-to-the-dvla-or-dva Supports: the doctor discloses to the DVLA medical adviser if the patient keeps driving when unfit and others are at risk of death or serious harm.
